title: CASE OF KOKY AND OTHERS v. SLOVAKIA
conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);Pecuniary damage - claim dismissed (Article 41 - Pecuniary damage);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage)
summary:
In Koky and Others v. Slovakia, the applicants were members of the Roma community living in the village of Gánovce-Filice, Slovakia. The case concerned the vulnerability of Roma residents who were subjected to a violent, racially motivated attack and the subsequent failure of the authorities to conduct an effective investigation. On the evening of 28 February 2002, following an argument in a local bar where a Roma man was refused service, a group of at least twelve masked and armed individuals entered the Roma settlement, shouting racist language, breaking into homes, damaging property, and physically assaulting several Roma residents, including Mr Ján Koky, Mr Martin Kočko, and Mr Rastislav Koky. Despite the serious nature of the attack and the injuries sustained, the police response was delayed and the ensuing investigation was inadequate, failing to identify or prosecute those responsible.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment, focusing on the procedural obligation to investigate such acts. The Court found a violation of Article 3 due to the authorities’ failure to carry out an effective investigation into the racially motivated violence. The applicants were awarded non-pecuniary damages as just satisfaction.

This judgment is significant as it highlights the persistent problem of anti-Roma violence and the duty of states to protect Roma and Traveller communities from racially motivated attacks, especially in light of Europe’s long history of discrimination against these groups.
